challenges.title: URL Shortener
challenges.problem: Design a service like bit.ly that turns long URLs into short codes and redirects visitors to the original URL. The system is extremely read-heavy: codes are created rarely but redirected to constantly, and redirects must feel instant.
functionalRequirements: Create a short code for a given long URL
Redirect a short code to its original URL
Serve a very high volume of redirects with low latency
constraints: Read:write ratio is roughly 100:1
Redirects should resolve in under ~50ms
Short codes are permanent once created

hints.title: Start at the edge
hints.body: Clients need a single HTTPS entry point. Put an API Gateway in front of your compute so every request lands in one place.

hints.title: Add compute logic
hints.body: API Gateway doesn't run code. Connect it to a compute service (like Lambda or ECS) to execute redirect and short code creation logic.

hints.title: Where do codes live?
hints.body: A code -> URL mapping is a simple key-value lookup. A NoSQL store like DynamoDB fits perfectly and scales easily.

hints.title: Make reads cheap
hints.body: 100:1 read-heavy workload means most lookups hit hot codes. Put ElastiCache (or CloudFront) in front of the database so requests never touch the database.

hints.title: Enable Observability
hints.body: Add a CloudWatch node to monitor your application's request latencies and check for traffic overload logs.

solution.summary: A URL shortener is read far more than it's written: a link is created once but clicked thousands of times. So the whole design is about making every click cheap and instant, while keeping 'create a link' simple.

requirementsMet.requirement: Create a short code for a long URL
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: When someone makes a link, the logic layer (Lambda) saves one simple entry, 'this short code points to that long URL', in the database. A create is just one quick write, so it stays cheap and easy.

requirementsMet.requirement: Redirect a short code to its original URL
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: On a click, the logic looks up the code (checking fast memory first, then the database) and sends the visitor straight to the original URL.

requirementsMet.requirement: Serve a very high volume of clicks with low latency
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: Most clicks are for the same popular links. The CDN answers many of them right next to the user, and a cache answers the rest in about a millisecond, so the database is barely touched. That is how it stays fast even at very high traffic.

services.name: DNS
services.role: Points your domain to an entry point.
services.why: It is the internet's address book. A managed one (Route 53) is reliable and points each visitor to the closest entry point, with nothing for you to run.

services.name: CDN
services.why: A redirect for a popular link is the same for everyone, so it can be reused. Serving it from a nearby location is faster for the user and takes load off everything behind it.

services.name: Redirect API
services.role: The single front door for all requests.
services.why: It gives you one secure entry point that grows with traffic on its own, so you never have to run or babysit web servers.

services.name: Redirect Fn
services.role: Creates and looks up short codes.
services.why: The work per request is tiny and comes in bursts. Code that runs only when needed scales instantly, and you pay per request instead of paying for idle servers.

services.name: Hot Code Cache
services.role: Remembers the most-clicked links in memory.
services.why: Reading from memory is much faster than reading from a database, and the same links get clicked over and over, so this answers most requests in about a millisecond. It speeds things up, but the database is still the real source of truth.

services.name: Code Store
services.why: Every lookup is just 'find by code', which this kind of database does extremely fast at any size with almost no setup. It keeps your data safe even though the cache serves most of the reads.

services.name: Monitoring
services.why: If something slows down or the cache stops working, you can see it here before your users ever feel it.

challenges.title: Celebrity Photo Feed
challenges.problem: A celebrity with 50 million followers posts a photo. Design the system that stores the post and delivers it to every follower's feed. The hard part is fan-out: a single write must reach millions of feeds without blocking the post request or melting the database.
functionalRequirements: Upload and store a photo
Record the post and fan it out to followers' feeds
Serve follower feeds quickly, even for celebrity-scale fan-out
constraints: One post can trigger millions of feed writes
The post request must not wait for fan-out to finish
Media reads vastly outnumber writes
challenges.targetScale: 50M followers per celebrity, heavy media read traffic

hints.title: API Gateway and Compute
hints.body: Configure a central API Gateway entry point and route posts/uploads to a compute handler (like Lambda or ECS).

hints.title: Store media separately
hints.body: Photos are large blobs - keep them in S3, not a database. Serve them through CloudFront so the origin isn't hammered.

hints.title: Decouple the write from the fan-out
hints.body: Don't update millions of feeds inside the post request. Publish an event to SNS/SQS (or EventBridge) and let workers fan out asynchronously.

hints.title: Persist follower feeds
hints.body: Create worker compute instances (ECS) that consume the queue events and write materialized feed lists into a DynamoDB database.

hints.title: Cache hot feeds
hints.body: A celebrity's feed is read constantly. Front the busiest feed databases with ElastiCache to cut database read load.

hints.title: Enable Observability
hints.body: Add a CloudWatch node to monitor workers queue performance and track fan-out lag statistics.

hints.title: Serve media through the CDN
hints.body: Point CloudFront at your S3 photo bucket so a popular image loads from a nearby edge instead of hitting storage on every view.

referenceSolution.notes: Synchronous post path stores media in S3 + metadata in DynamoDB, then publishes to SNS→SQS for async worker fan-out into a feed store, with ElastiCache fronting hot feeds and CloudFront serving media.

solution.summary: Reading a feed must feel instant, but one celebrity post has to reach millions of feeds. The trick is to split the work: store the post and reply right away, then fan it out to followers in the background so nobody waits on the slow part.

requirementsMet.requirement: Upload and store a photo
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: The image is saved as a file in object storage (S3) and served from nearby edge locations (CloudFront), so the upload is one write and every later view is fast.

requirementsMet.requirement: Record the post and fan it out to followers' feeds
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: The post is written once to a database (DynamoDB), then a single announcement goes onto a topic and queue (SNS to SQS). Background workers copy it into each follower's feed without holding up the poster.

requirementsMet.requirement: Serve follower feeds quickly, even for celebrity-scale fan-out
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: Each follower's feed is built ahead of time and stored (DynamoDB), and the hottest feeds are kept in memory (ElastiCache), so opening a feed is a simple, instant read.

challenges.title: Pastebin
challenges.problem: Design a service where users paste text or code and get a short shareable link to view it later. Most pastes are written once and read many times, and some expire after a set time.

Fetch a paste by its id
Support optional expiry (TTL) on pastes
constraints: Reads far outnumber writes
Pastes are immutable once created
Large pastes shouldn't bloat the primary database
challenges.targetScale: Millions of stored pastes, heavily read-skewed traffic

hints.title: Where does text live?
hints.body: Store paste metadata and short text in DynamoDB (great for key lookups, and TTL handles expiry). Keep very large pastes as objects in S3.

hints.title: Make reads cheap
hints.body: Pastes are immutable and read-heavy, so they cache perfectly. Put CloudFront (or ElastiCache) in front so popular pastes skip the database.

hints.title: Enable observability
hints.body: Add a CloudWatch node to watch request latency and error rates.

solution.summary: A paste is written once and read many times, so the design keeps writing simple and makes reading cheap and global. Small pastes live in a fast database, big ones go to file storage, and expiry is handled automatically.

challenges.title: API Rate Limiter
challenges.problem: Design a distributed rate limiter that caps how many requests each client can make in a time window. It must work across many API servers, so the counter can't live in a single server's memory.
functionalRequirements: Count requests per client per time window
Allow or reject a request based on its limit
Share counts consistently across all API instances
constraints: Limit checks must add minimal latency
Counters must be consistent across servers
Limits differ per client and per route
challenges.targetScale: Tens of thousands of checks/sec across many instances

hints.title: One entry point
hints.body: Front everything with an API Gateway so every request passes one checkpoint.

hints.title: Evaluate the limit in compute
hints.body: Connect the gateway to a compute service (Lambda or ECS) that decides allow vs reject for each request.

hints.title: Counters can't be local
hints.body: If each server keeps counts in its own memory, the limit breaks behind a load balancer. Use a fast shared store like ElastiCache (Redis) for atomic per-client counters.

hints.title: Read counters from compute
hints.body: On each request, have your compute atomically read and increment the client's counter in ElastiCache, then allow or reject. (Keep per-client limit rules in DynamoDB so they change without a redeploy.)

hints.title: Enable observability
hints.body: Add CloudWatch to track rejection rates and counter latency.

solution.summary: Every request must be checked in well under a millisecond, and the count has to be the same no matter which server handles it. So the counters live in one shared in-memory store that every instance reads and updates, not in any single server's memory.

requirementsMet.requirement: Count requests per client per time window
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: Each client's count lives in a shared in-memory store (ElastiCache). Bumping a counter there is a single fast step, and the window resets on its own with an expiry.

requirementsMet.requirement: Allow or reject a request based on its limit
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: The check logic (Lambda) increases the client's counter and compares it to that client's limit, allowing or rejecting instantly.

requirementsMet.requirement: Share counts consistently across all API instances
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: Because the counter lives in one central store (ElastiCache) instead of any server's memory, every API instance sees the same number, so the limit holds across the whole fleet.

services.name: Limiter Fn

services.why: The decision is tiny and runs once per request, so code that runs only when needed (Lambda) scales instantly with traffic and costs nothing when idle.

services.name: Counter Cache
services.role: Holds each client's live request count.
services.why: Counting has to be fast and shared, and an in-memory store (ElastiCache) bumps counters in about a millisecond with automatic window expiry, which a disk database can't match at this rate.

services.name: Limit Policies
services.why: Limits change rarely and are read by key, so a simple, durable database (DynamoDB) holds them while the cache stays focused on fast counting.

services.name: Monitoring
services.why: Spikes in rejections or slow checks show up here (CloudWatch) so you can spot abuse or trouble early.

challenges.title: Real-time Notifications
challenges.problem: Design a system that delivers real-time notifications (messages, mentions, alerts) to millions of connected clients. Producers must not block waiting for every device to receive the event.
functionalRequirements: Authenticate connected users
Track which users and devices are currently online
Deliver notifications to recipients in near real-time
Decouple event producers from delivery workers
constraints: Millions of concurrent connections
Producers must not block on delivery
A recipient may be offline and reconnect later

hints.title: Decouple producers from delivery
hints.body: Publish notification events to SNS/SQS (or EventBridge) so producers return instantly and never wait on delivery.

hints.title: Delivery workers
hints.body: Run worker compute (ECS) that consumes the queue and pushes notifications to connected clients, updating delivery state.

hints.title: Enable observability
hints.body: Add CloudWatch to monitor queue depth and fan-out lag.

solution.summary: The goal is to reach millions of connected devices the instant something happens, without making the sender wait. Events are published once and handed to background workers, while a registry tracks who is online and where to send each message.

requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: Sign-in and tokens are handled by a managed identity service (Cognito), so only verified users open a connection and you don't build auth yourself.

requirementsMet.requirement: Decouple event producers from delivery workers

challenges.title: Video Streaming Platform
challenges.problem: Design a global video platform: users upload videos, the system transcodes them into multiple resolutions, and viewers stream them smoothly anywhere in the world.
functionalRequirements: Accept large video uploads
Transcode uploads into multiple bitrates asynchronously
Store and globally deliver video segments
Track a catalog of videos and their processing status
constraints: Uploads are large; transcoding is slow and bursty
Viewers vastly outnumber uploaders
Playback must start fast for a global audience

hints.body: Add CloudWatch to watch transcode backlog and playback errors.

hints.title: Serve segments through the CDN

challenges.title: Distributed Job Scheduler
challenges.problem: Design a service that schedules millions of delayed and recurring jobs and runs them reliably, triggering at the right time, retrying failures, and never losing a job.
functionalRequirements: Accept and store job definitions and their schedules
Trigger jobs at the right time (delayed and recurring)
Execute jobs reliably with retries
Decouple scheduling from execution
constraints: Millions of scheduled jobs
At-least-once execution, so no lost jobs
Execution load is spiky
challenges.targetScale: Millions of scheduled jobs, spiky execution bursts

hints.title: Submit jobs through an API
hints.body: Expose an API Gateway to a compute handler (Lambda or ECS) that accepts new job definitions and schedules.

hints.title: Store job definitions
hints.body: Persist every job and its schedule in a durable database like DynamoDB so nothing is lost.

hints.title: Trigger on time
hints.body: Use EventBridge as a time-based scheduler to fire due jobs into compute, both one-off delays and recurring cron-style runs.

hints.title: Decouple dispatch with a queue
hints.body: Push due jobs onto a durable queue (SQS). The queue absorbs spikes and guarantees a job isn't lost if a worker dies.

hints.title: Worker fleet executes
hints.body: Run worker compute (ECS or Lambda) that pulls from the queue, executes with retries, and writes status back. Use Step Functions for jobs with several dependent steps.

hints.title: Enable observability
hints.body: Add CloudWatch to watch the due-job backlog and execution failure rates.

referenceSolution.notes: Submit path (API → Lambda → DynamoDB) stores schedules. EventBridge fires a dispatcher Lambda that enqueues due jobs to SQS; ECS workers execute and update status, with Step Functions orchestrating multi-step jobs.

solution.summary: A scheduler must fire jobs at exactly the right time and never lose one, even at millions of jobs. So schedules are stored durably, a time-based trigger wakes due jobs, and running is kept separate from scheduling so retries don't hold anything up.

requirementsMet.requirement: Accept and store job definitions and their schedules
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: Submitted jobs are written to a durable database (DynamoDB), so a job is safe the moment it's accepted.

requirementsMet.requirement: Trigger jobs at the right time (delayed and recurring)
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: A managed time-based trigger (EventBridge) wakes on schedule and a dispatcher (Lambda) finds the jobs that are now due, handling both one-off delays and repeats.

requirementsMet.requirement: Execute jobs reliably with retries
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: Due jobs go onto a queue (SQS) and are run by workers (ECS); multi-step jobs use a workflow (Step Functions) that retries failed steps, and a job stays on the queue until it succeeds, so nothing is lost.

requirementsMet.requirement: Decouple scheduling from execution
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: Scheduling just drops due jobs on the queue; workers consume them separately, so slow or failing jobs never block the scheduler from firing the next ones.

challenges.title: Gaming Leaderboard
challenges.problem: Design a real-time leaderboard that ranks millions of players by score. Players' scores change constantly, and the app must instantly show the global top N as well as any single player's rank and the players just above and below them.
functionalRequirements: Update a player's score after each match
Return the global top N players instantly
Return a single player's current rank and nearby players
constraints: Rank and top-N queries must resolve in under ~50ms
Scores update heavily during peak hours
Reads (viewing ranks) far outnumber writes (score updates)
challenges.targetScale: Millions of players, tens of thousands of score updates/sec at peak

hints.title: One entry point
hints.body: Give clients a single HTTPS entry point with an API Gateway so every score update and rank query lands in one place.

hints.title: Add compute logic
hints.body: API Gateway can't run code. Connect it to a compute service (Lambda or ECS) that processes score updates and answers rank queries.

hints.title: Pick the right ranking structure
hints.body: A relational table can't sort millions of rows per keystroke. Use ElastiCache (Redis) sorted sets: O(log n) score updates and instant top-N and rank lookups straight from memory.

hints.title: Don't lose scores
hints.body: Redis is the fast ranking layer, not the source of truth. Persist authoritative scores in DynamoDB so the leaderboard can be rebuilt if the cache is lost.

hints.title: Enable observability
hints.body: Add a CloudWatch node to track query latency and update throughput.

hints.title: Rank through the cache
hints.body: Have compute read and update ranks directly in the in-memory store (ElastiCache/Redis) so top-N and a single player's rank come back in about a millisecond.

challenges.title: Search Autocomplete
challenges.problem: Design a search autocomplete (typeahead) service that returns the top suggestions for whatever prefix a user has typed so far, within a few milliseconds per keystroke. Suggestions are ranked by popularity and must stay fresh as search trends shift, without ever slowing down the live read path.
functionalRequirements: Return the top suggestions for a given prefix with very low latency
Log every executed search query
Rebuild ranked suggestions from query frequency over time
Keep the fast read path independent from the heavy rebuild path
constraints: A suggestion lookup fires on every keystroke and must return in a few ms
The system ingests a massive, continuous stream of query logs
Suggestion rankings change as trends shift
The rebuild must never slow the live read path
challenges.targetScale: Tens of thousands of prefix lookups/sec; billions of query events ingested

hints.title: Read path entry
hints.body: Front the lookups with an API Gateway routed to a compute handler (Lambda or ECS) that answers prefix queries.

hints.title: Serve prefixes from memory
hints.body: A database query per keystroke is far too slow. Keep precomputed top-K suggestions per prefix in ElastiCache (Redis) so each lookup is a single in-memory read.

hints.title: Capture the query stream
hints.body: Every executed search is an event. Stream raw queries into Kinesis so ingestion scales independently from the read path and the producer never blocks.

hints.title: Aggregate asynchronously
hints.body: Run worker compute that consumes the stream, counts prefix frequencies, and stores ranked suggestions durably in DynamoDB.

hints.title: Refresh the cache
hints.body: Have the rebuild write the new top-K per prefix back into ElastiCache, so the read path always serves fresh, precomputed results without touching the aggregation pipeline.

hints.title: Enable observability
hints.body: Add CloudWatch to watch ingestion lag and the cache hit rate.

hints.title: Log every query
hints.body: Write each search the lookup path receives onto the stream (Kinesis) so the background aggregator can rebuild rankings from real query frequency.

referenceSolution.notes: Read path (API → Suggest Handler → ElastiCache) answers each keystroke from precomputed top-K. The handler also logs queries to a Kinesis stream; an Aggregator consumes the stream, persists ranked suggestions to DynamoDB, and refreshes the prefix cache.

solution.summary: Every keystroke needs an answer in a few milliseconds, while suggestions stay fresh as trends shift. So the read path just looks up pre-computed results in memory, and a separate background pipeline rebuilds the rankings, keeping the two from slowing each other down.

requirementsMet.requirement: Return the top suggestions for a given prefix with very low latency
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: Pre-computed suggestions for each prefix are held in memory (ElastiCache), so a keystroke is answered in about a millisecond with no heavy computation.

requirementsMet.requirement: Log every executed search query
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: Each search is written to a streaming pipeline (Kinesis) that can absorb a firehose of events without slowing the user's request.

requirementsMet.requirement: Rebuild ranked suggestions from query frequency over time
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: A background job (Lambda) reads the stream, tallies how often queries appear, and rewrites the ranked suggestions (DynamoDB), refreshing the in-memory cache as trends change.

requirementsMet.requirement: Keep the fast read path independent from the heavy rebuild path
requirementsMet.satisfiedBy: Typing only ever reads the cache, while counting and re-ranking happen entirely on the streaming side, so the expensive rebuild never slows down live suggestions.

services.why: Tallying frequencies and re-ranking is periodic batch work that fits code that runs only when needed (Lambda), kept well away from the live read path.

services.name: Suggestions Store
services.why: The computed rankings live in a durable database (DynamoDB) so they survive restarts and can refill the cache.

services.name: Monitoring
services.why: If lookups slow down or the rebuild stalls, you can see it here (CloudWatch) before users get stale or sluggish suggestions.
